reference.source: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
clinicalPearls: A thin mucosal membrane, usually anterior and eccentric, projecting into the oesophageal lumen, most often in the upper (cervical) oesophagus
Composed of mucosa and submucosa only, unlike the muscular ring at the lower oesophagus
Typically causes intermittent dysphagia to solids and can be asymptomatic when the lumen is only mildly narrowed
Upper oesophageal (post-cricoid) webs are classically associated with iron-deficiency anaemia in Plummer-Vinson syndrome
Best demonstrated on a well-timed barium swallow, as thin webs can be missed or ruptured at endoscopy
Management is endoscopic disruption or dilatation of symptomatic webs, together with correction of underlying iron deficiency where present
May be congenital or acquired and can be associated with mucocutaneous or autoimmune conditions
reference.pathophysiology: An oesophageal web is a thin, shelf-like protrusion of mucosa and submucosa that partially occludes the lumen. Webs may be congenital or acquired, the latter linked to chronic iron deficiency, mucosal inflammation, and certain immune-mediated dermatoses. The membrane narrows the effective luminal diameter, so that bolus transit of solids is intermittently obstructed, producing dysphagia; because the wall muscle is not involved, peristalsis is preserved and symptoms depend chiefly on the degree of luminal compromise.
additionalInvestigations: Barium swallow with attention to the cervical oesophagus and dynamic images
Upper endoscopy for direct visualisation and therapeutic disruption
Full blood count and iron studies to detect associated iron deficiency
Oesophageal biopsies to exclude eosinophilic oesophagitis or malignancy
Assessment for associated mucocutaneous or autoimmune disease when suspected
redFlags: Progressive rather than intermittent dysphagia suggesting stricture or malignancy
Post-cricoid web with iron deficiency, given the increased risk of hypopharyngeal cancer
reference.prognosis: Symptomatic webs generally respond well to endoscopic disruption or dilatation, though they can recur; the main concern with post-cricoid webs is the associated long-term risk of hypopharyngeal squamous carcinoma.
pitfalls: Missing a thin web on endoscopy because it ruptures on scope passage
Failing to recognise and treat the associated iron deficiency
Attributing dysphagia to a web without excluding malignancy
Confusing a proximal web with a distal Schatzki ring
